title: Reconstructing Scots pine stem taper using mobile laser scanning data from the lower stem
content:
Abstract
Terrestrial close-range remote sensing enables detailed 3D tree characterization, but crown occlusion complicates upper-stem diameter estimation. Conventional taper models often require tree height, which may be unavailable or inaccurate under operational forest conditions. We evaluated how the extent of lower-stem diameter profiles derived from mobile laser scanning (MLS) affects taper reconstruction in a managed boreal Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) stand. Diameter profiles extending to 2, 5, and 7 m above the stem base were used in a multivariate taper model that exploits covariances among stem dimensions to reconstruct taper without measured tree height. Reconstruction performance was evaluated against field calliper measurements and height-dependent benchmarks. Across 64 trees, MLS-derived diameter estimates had a root mean square error (RMSE) of 10.8 mm. At 6 m, diameter prediction RMSE decreased from 19.6 mm (relative RMSE: 8.9%) using diameter at breast height (DBH) alone to 9.4 mm (4.3%) using the 2 m profile and to 6.5 mm (2.9%) using the 5 m profile. Relative RMSE for reconstructed tree height decreased from 19.3% with DBH alone to 12.6%, 10.7%, and 9.5% for the 2, 5, and 7 m profiles, respectively. The height-dependent benchmark using calliper DBH and measured tree height gave a diameter RMSE of 11.9 mm at 6 m, while perturbing tree height by +1 and −1 m changed the RMSE to 11.0 and 13.1 mm, respectively. In an independent sample of three Scots pines with destructive reference profiles, the RMSE of predicted diameters above 7 m decreased from 55.5 mm with DBH alone to 34.5, 22.5, and 14.1 mm with the 2, 5, and 7 m diameter profiles, respectively. The largest improvement was achieved by extending the input from DBH alone to the 2 m profile. These results support reconstructing stem taper from MLS-derived lower-stem profiles when reliable tree height is unavailable.
